# Display Interface — GFX HAT

## Overview

The machine interface is implemented with a **Pimoroni GFX HAT** connected to the Raspberry Pi 3. The board combines:

- a 128 × 64 monochrome LCD display;
- six capacitive touch buttons;
- RGB backlighting;
- six button indicator LEDs.

The display is used as a small human-machine interface (HMI): the user can select a `.png` pattern stored on a USB drive, prepare the yarns, start or stop the process, check the progress percentage, and receive interruption messages.

The user interface is implemented in:

```text
gfxhat_pattern_ui.py
```

At the current prototype stage, the program can already be tested in **demo mode**: the progress bar and all alarm screens can be checked without connecting the motors, the ESP32, or the error-recognition pipeline.

> The current script manages the display workflow and the USB pattern selection. Motor actuation and real camera-triggered alerts must later be connected through the `MachineController` methods and the notification functions already provided in the script.

---

## System Role

The Raspberry Pi is responsible for the high-level interface and vision tasks, while the ESP32 will manage time-critical motion control.

```text
PC user
└── Pattern Editor → saves one or more .png files on a USB drive

Knitting machine
├── Raspberry Pi 3
│   ├── GFX HAT interface
│   ├── USB pattern loading
│   ├── Pi Camera error recognition
│   └── progress and alarm management
│
└── ESP32
    ├── stepper motor driver
    ├── three colour-selection servos
    └── synchronization microswitch
```

In the final system, the ESP32 will inform the Raspberry Pi whenever a synchronized control instant is reached. The Raspberry Pi can then run the vision check and update the interface.

---

## GFX HAT and Pi Camera Connection

The GFX HAT and the Pi Camera can be used at the same time because they are connected through different interfaces:

```text
GFX HAT   → Raspberry Pi GPIO header
Pi Camera → Raspberry Pi CSI camera connector
```

The GFX HAT uses both **SPI** and **I²C** communication. According to the Pimoroni pinout documentation, it requires 5 V and 3.3 V power, uses 7 GPIO communication pins, and includes the I²C devices `CAP1166` for the touch buttons and `SN3218` for the RGB backlight.

If the HAT is mounted directly on the Raspberry Pi and obstructs the camera flat cable, the display can be connected through a **40-pin GPIO extension cable** or an extra-tall stacking header. This also allows the display to be installed on the external control panel of the machine, while the Raspberry Pi remains protected inside the enclosure.

### Minimum Wiring when the Display is Remote

When using individual wires instead of a full 40-pin extension cable, connect the following pins:

| Function | Raspberry Pi GPIO | Physical pin |
|---|---:|---:|
| 3.3 V power | 3V3 | 1 |
| 5 V power | 5V | 2 |
| Ground | GND | 6 |
| Touch/backlight data | GPIO 2 / SDA | 3 |
| Touch/backlight clock | GPIO 3 / SCL | 5 |
| LCD data | GPIO 10 / SPI MOSI | 19 |
| LCD clock | GPIO 11 / SPI SCLK | 23 |
| LCD chip select | GPIO 8 / SPI CE0 | 24 |
| LCD reset | GPIO 5 | 29 |
| LCD data/command | GPIO 6 | 31 |

A full 40-pin GPIO extension cable is recommended over individual jumper wires, since it reduces wiring errors and preserves the correct pin orientation.

## Interface Workflow

The interface implements the following workflow:

```text
USB drive inserted
        ↓
Select a PNG pattern using the touch buttons
        ↓
Selected pattern is copied locally to the Raspberry Pi
        ↓
"INSERIRE I FILATI" screen
        ↓
User presses AVVIA
        ↓
Progress screen with percentage and completed cycles
        ↓
Possible interruptions:
    - "ERRORE RISCONTRATO"
    - "TAGLIARE IL FILO"
        ↓
User corrects the problem and presses AVVIA to resume
        ↓
"LAVORO COMPLETATO"
```

Once a file is selected, it is copied from the USB drive to:

```text
~/automated_knitting_machine/patterns/current_pattern.png
```

This prevents an accidental USB removal from interrupting a process that has already started.

---

## Touch Button Mapping

The six GFX HAT touch buttons are used as follows:

| Touch button | Function in the user interface |
|---|---|
| `UP` | Move to the previous `.png` file |
| `DOWN` | Move to the next `.png` file |
| `SELECT` | Confirm the selected pattern |
| `PLUS` | Refresh the USB list / start / resume |
| `MINUS` | Stop the process |
| `BACK` | Return to the pattern menu |

During **demo mode**, two buttons are additionally used to simulate machine events while the progress screen is active:

| Touch button | Demo action |
|---|---|
| `BACK` | Simulate `ERRORE RISCONTRATO` |
| `SELECT` | Simulate `TAGLIARE IL FILO` |

---

## Interface Screens

### Pattern Selection

When the program starts, it reads the `.png` files contained in the mounted USB folder and displays a scrollable list:

```text
SELEZIONA PNG

> cuore.png
  righe.png
  fiore.png

^v SPOSTA  OK SEL  + REF
```

If no PNG file is found, the interface displays:

```text
NESSUN FILE PNG
INSERIRE USB

+ AGGIORNA
```

### Yarn Preparation

After selecting a pattern, the user is asked to insert the correct yarns:

```text
PATTERN SELEZIONATO
cuore.png

INSERIRE
I FILATI

+ AVVIA    < MENU
```

### Processing Screen

Once the job starts, the display shows its status and progress:

```text
cuore.png

IN LAVORAZIONE

[ progress bar ]

36%   18/50

- STOP
```

### Interruption Screens

When the vision system detects a defect, the program can call:

```python
app.notify_error()
```

The interface then shows:

```text
ERRORE
RISCONTRATO

FERMO AL 36%

+ RIPRENDI  < MENU
```

When a colour-distance condition requires manual yarn cutting, the program can call:

```python
app.notify_cut_thread()
```

The interface then shows:

```text
TAGLIARE
IL FILO

FERMO AL 36%

+ RIPRENDI  < MENU
```

In both cases, the user can resolve the problem and press `PLUS` to resume.

## Raspberry Pi Setup

The current Raspberry Pi is used in **headless mode**, through SSH. Therefore, all installation and testing steps are executed from the terminal.

### 1. Enable SPI and I²C

The GFX HAT needs both SPI and I²C enabled.

Connect to the Raspberry Pi through SSH and run:

```bash
sudo raspi-config
```

Navigate to:

```text
Interface Options
├── SPI → Enable
└── I2C → Enable
```

Then reboot:

```bash
sudo reboot
```

After reconnecting through SSH, SPI can be checked with:

```bash
ls /dev/spidev*
```

The I²C bus can be checked by installing `i2c-tools` and scanning bus 1:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y i2c-tools
sudo i2cdetect -y 1
```

With the GFX HAT connected, the touch controller and backlight controller are expected at addresses:

```text
0x2c  → CAP1166 touch controller
0x54  → SN3218 RGB backlight controller
```

---

## Python Environment and Library Installation

Because recent Raspberry Pi OS versions protect the system Python environment, the project uses a Python virtual environment.

Install the required system packages:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3-venv python3-pil python3-rpi.gpio python3-spidev python3-smbus i2c-tools
```

Create the virtual environment, if it does not already exist:

```bash
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages ~/venvs/uncinetto
```

Activate it:

```bash
source ~/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate
```

The terminal prompt should now start with:

```text
(uncinetto)
```

Install the GFX HAT Python library inside the virtual environment:

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install gfxhat
```

The Pimoroni `gfxhat` package installs the Python interface to the LCD, RGB backlight and touch controls; its package dependencies include the `cap1xxx` and `sn3218` drivers.

## USB Drive Setup

The user creates the pattern on a personal computer using the Pattern Editor and saves one or more `.png` files to a USB drive.

Example USB content:

```text
USB_DRIVE/
├── cuore.png
├── fiore.png
└── righe.png
```

### 1. Identify the USB Partition

Insert the USB drive into the Raspberry Pi and run:

```bash
lsblk
```

In the current prototype test, the USB drive was recognized as:

```text
sda
└─sda1
```

Therefore, the partition to mount is:

```text
/dev/sda1
```

### 2. Mount the USB Drive

Create a fixed mount directory:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/pattern_usb
```

Mount the USB partition:

```bash
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/pattern_usb
```

If the terminal displays the following warning:

```text
mount: (hint) your fstab has been modified, but systemd still uses
       the old version; use 'systemctl daemon-reload' to reload.
```

run:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```

Then verify that the USB drive is correctly mounted:

```bash
findmnt /mnt/pattern_usb
ls -lah /mnt/pattern_usb
```

The `.png` files should appear in the directory listing.

### 3. Safely Remove the USB Drive

Before physically removing the USB drive, stop the program and unmount it:

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/pattern_usb
```

---

## Running `gfxhat_pattern_ui.py`

In the current prototype, the script is stored in the user home directory:

```text
/home/aless/gfxhat_pattern_ui.py
```

Activate the environment before running it:

```bash
source ~/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate
```

### Demo Mode

Demo mode is used to test the display, the USB file selection, the touch buttons, the progress screen and the two interruption screens without starting any real actuator:

```bash
python3 ~/gfxhat_pattern_ui.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb --demo
```

Test sequence:

```text
UP / DOWN  → browse the available PNG files
SELECT     → choose one PNG file
PLUS       → start the simulated process
MINUS      → stop the process
PLUS       → resume the process
BACK       → simulate "ERRORE RISCONTRATO" while running
SELECT     → simulate "TAGLIARE IL FILO" while running
```

In demo mode, the progress percentage automatically increases until the completion screen is displayed.

### Real Mode

The program can also be started without the simulator:

```bash
python3 ~/gfxhat_pattern_ui.py --usb-dir /mnt/pattern_usb
```

In this mode, the interface operates normally, but the progress percentage will not increase until the real machine-control code sends progress events.

## Software Integration with the Machine

The interface code already exposes the methods required by the future control pipeline.

### Progress Update

The real control code must notify the interface whenever a cycle or a row is completed:

```python
app.notify_progress(completed_cycles, total_cycles)
```

Example:

```python
app.notify_progress(18, 50)
```

The display will report:

```text
36%   18/50
```

### Error Recognition Alert

When the Raspberry Pi camera classifier detects an error in the yarn or in the manufactured structure, the vision code must call:

```python
app.notify_error()
```

This opens the `ERRORE RISCONTRATO` screen and requests a pause of the machine.

### Long-Distance Yarn Cut Alert

When the pattern-processing logic detects a distance that requires manual cutting of a yarn, it must call:

```python
app.notify_cut_thread()
```

This opens the `TAGLIARE IL FILO` screen.

### Completion Event

When the machine completes the selected pattern, the controller must call:

```python
app.notify_done()
```

### ESP32 Communication

The class:

```python
MachineController
```

contains the methods that will later be connected to the ESP32 through USB serial communication:

```python
start()
stop()
pause()
resume()
```

At present these methods only print terminal messages. In the final control system, they will send real commands to the ESP32, which will control the stepper motor, the three servos and the synchronization microswitch.

## Compatibility Fix: `lcd.contrast()`

During the first execution on the Raspberry Pi, the following error occurred:

```text
AttributeError: module 'gfxhat.lcd' has no attribute 'contrast'
```

The error was generated by this line in `GfxScreen.__init__()`:

```python
lcd.contrast(42)
```

Some installed versions of the `gfxhat` Python library do not expose the `contrast()` function through `gfxhat.lcd`. To keep the application compatible with both versions, the script was corrected as follows:

```python
lcd.clear()
if hasattr(lcd, "contrast"):
    lcd.contrast(42)
self.set_backlight((0, 40, 70))
```

With this modification, contrast is set only when the function is available; otherwise, the program continues normally using the default contrast.

---

## Troubleshooting

### No PNG Files Are Displayed

Check that the USB drive is mounted and contains `.png` files directly in its root folder:

```bash
findmnt /mnt/pattern_usb
ls -lah /mnt/pattern_usb
```

Then press the `PLUS` touch button on the file-selection screen to refresh the list.

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gfxhat'`

Activate the correct virtual environment and install the package:

```bash
source ~/venvs/uncinetto/bin/activate
python -m pip install gfxhat
```

### Display or Touch Buttons Do Not Respond

Verify that SPI and I²C are enabled:

```bash
ls /dev/spidev*
sudo i2cdetect -y 1
```

The I²C scan should identify the GFX HAT control devices at `0x2c` and `0x54`. Also verify the GPIO cable orientation if the HAT is connected through an extension cable.

### `AttributeError: module 'gfxhat.lcd' has no attribute 'contrast'`

Make sure that the initialization of `GfxScreen` contains the compatibility condition:

```python
lcd.clear()
if hasattr(lcd, "contrast"):
    lcd.contrast(42)
self.set_backlight((0, 40, 70))
```

### USB Removal

Do not remove the USB drive while it is still mounted. Once the program is stopped, run:

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/pattern_usb
```

## Future Development

The GFX HAT interface already defines the complete expected operator workflow. The following integrations remain to be completed:

- connection of `MachineController` to the ESP32 through USB serial communication;
- update of the progress counter from the physical synchronization events;
- connection of the Pi Camera recognition output to `notify_error()`;
- detection of long yarn distances and activation of `notify_cut_thread()`;
- automatic start of the user interface when the Raspberry Pi is powered on.
